doc.title: Vince Lateano interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Royalties, sidemen and the Jimmy Cobb example
summary: Sidemen are paid for the date only; Cobb made little on the most famous jazz record.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: As a sideman on that record do you get anything?
I got a hearty handshake.
Yeah, right. It’d be nice if you got like a certificate or something.
Well you know Carl Jefferson from Concord Records gave us each plaques.
Yeah.
You know.
Okay.
Commemoration. That’s cool. Hey man, that’s how it works, you know?
Do you ever get — I don’t know if royalties is the right word.
That’s the right word. No. I don’t have any tunes, any publishing.
Okay. But so just for playing on things you don’t get it.
Yeah. You get paid for the date.
Right.
I mean look at what the — Jimmy Cobb. You know? He’s on probably the most famous jazz record in the world and I think he made a couple hundred bucks or something.
Right. That is amazing to think of that.
Yeah. Jimmy Cobb is another one of my favorites. Boy I love that guy.
Re-issued and there’ve been books about it.
I know. And movies.
God. You can’t eat fame though.

You know I mean you sort of know that going in. I mean I guess some guys get bitter about it. But if your name isn’t on the sign, I mean if you’re not the leader, it’s just like you know you contributed somehow, you were there, and your presence, but it just doesn’t seem to work that way.
